name: Bruin
license: Apache 2.0 (the CLI, since its first commit in 2023); the ingestr engine it installs is FSL-1.1-ALv2 since its 2026 Go rewrite (each release becomes Apache 2.0 after two years; earlier Python versions are MIT); Bruin Cloud is proprietary
summary: One Go command-line tool that ingests data, runs SQL and Python transformations and checks the results, with each step a file in your repo.
intro: A Bruin project is a git repository. `.bruin.yml` at the root holds environments and connection credentials; each pipeline folder has a `pipeline.yml` and an `assets/` folder, and every asset is one file. A SQL asset starts with a `/* @bruin ... @bruin */` YAML header giving the table name, the platform (`duckdb.sql`, `bigquery.sql`, `snowflake.sql` and so on), how to materialize it (table, view or an incremental strategy such as merge) and its upstream `depends`. Python assets carry the same kind of header and run in their own `uv` environment. An `ingestr` asset copies a table from a source connection into the warehouse. `bruin run` executes assets in dependency order, inside your warehouse, and after each one runs its column checks (`not_null`, `unique`, `non_negative`, custom SQL); a failing blocking check stops everything downstream. `bruin lineage` shows upstream and downstream assets, and the SQL parser can trace lineage down to columns.

The CLI keeps no server and no scheduler: you run it on a laptop, a VM or GitHub Actions, and the `schedule` in `pipeline.yml` is read by Bruin Cloud or your own scheduler. Bruin Data Limited, an English company incorporated in June 2023, builds it alongside ingestr, its ingestion engine. Bruin Cloud bills per second at $0.01 per credit: SQL assets, and Python or ingestion assets on the default 256 MB size, cost 250 credits ($2.50) an hour, rising to $160 an hour at 16 GB, and AI tasks cost 100 to 300 credits each. New accounts get $100 of credits; the Scale plan adds committed-use discounts, SSO and an SLA.
strengths: Ingestion, transformation, quality checks and lineage in one tool and one file format, instead of three or four products glued together
A single Go binary with no server, so the same pipeline runs locally and in CI
Wide platform support: 28 warehouse and lake platforms (BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, DuckDB, Postgres, ClickHouse, Trino and more) and over 130 ingestion sources
SQL, Python and R assets in the same pipeline, with Python isolated per asset by `uv`
Apache 2.0 CLI and an open-source VS Code extension that renders queries, lineage and checks
limits: Young: still version 0.x after three years, with releases almost daily (0.11.773 on 6 October 2026) and a small community next to Airbyte or dbt
The ingestion engine is not plain open source any more: ingestr 1.x is under the Functional Source License, which bars competing uses until each release turns Apache 2.0 after two years
No scheduler or retry service in the CLI: production scheduling means Bruin Cloud, cron, GitHub Actions or another orchestrator
Assets use Bruin’s own comment-header format, so pipelines do not move to dbt or Airflow without rewriting
Lakehouse support (Iceberg and DuckLake through DuckDB or Trino) is still marked beta

story: Burak Karakan and Sabri Karagönen started Bruin Data in 2023, incorporating in England that June. Their complaint was the modern data stack itself: one tool to ingest, another to transform, another to check quality, another to orchestrate, and a pile of glue between them. Karakan’s launch post sketches the setup teams typically described: Airflow triggering Airbyte and waiting on sensors, calling dbt Cloud, spinning up pods for checks, while analysts wait six weeks for a new chart.

The first commit landed in July 2023 and v0.1.0 was tagged that December. In early 2024 the team split ingestion out as ingestr, a command-line tool that copies a table from a source URI to a destination URI, first written in Python on top of dlt. Bruin CLI and its VS Code extension were launched publicly in December 2024, with a hosted Bruin Cloud announced alongside.
In 2026 ingestr was rewritten in Go for version 1.0 and moved from MIT to the Functional Source License, while the Bruin CLI stayed Apache 2.0.

choices.choice: One tool for ingestion, transformation and quality
choices.why: The founders saw most breakages and delays in the glue between separate products, and argued that work which belongs together should live in one framework.

choices.choice: Assets as files with an embedded YAML header
choices.why: Keeping configuration next to the SQL or Python in the same file means the whole pipeline is versioned, reviewed and run from a git repo.
A single static binary is easy to install anywhere, from a laptop to GitHub Actions, without a Python environment for the CLI itself.
